question: Dozens of unions representing healthcare workers are mobilising in light of the criminal bill put forward by the New Democracy government, which privatises public mental health, drug prevention and rehabilitation services. The plan, under this bill, is to close two of the three remaining psychiatric hospitals in the country (the psychiatric hospitals of Attica and Thessaloniki).

The bill also advocates the closure of the KETHEA addiction treatment centres and the drug rehabilitation programmes 18 ANO, ARGO, IANOS and DIAPLOUS and terminates prevention centres, since it does not guarantee that they will go on functioning beyond 2027. In view of this, can the Commission say what its position is concerning the fact that: 1.

While more and more people are experiencing mental health problems, the implementation of EU policy – which involves closing down public psychiatric institutions, undermining prevention and weakening and underfunding public structures – is leading to greater commercialisation and to public mental health services being handed over to private parties, NGOs and civil non-profit companies (AMKE) using the Recovery Fund as a tool and sacrificing the needs of mentally ill people?

While EU policy is leading to an increase in substance dependence, the direct consequence of discontinuing ‘dry’ treatment programmes and prevention centres is that it hurts structures that stand out to this day for their effectiveness and major contribution in tackling the problem?

In both the mental health and substance rehabilitation sectors, the EU guidelines upheld in the bill in question are leading thousands of workers into unemployment as if they were expendable, while those who get to keep their jobs face a drastic deterioration in labour relations and the explosion of flexible, badly paid work?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.10.2024) According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, the definition of national health policy and the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care including in the field of mental health, is a national competence.
The Commission supports Member States in strengthening their health workforce via the EU4Health, Erasmus+ and the Third Health Programme.

Examples are a joint action on forecasting and planning of health workforce2; projects on workforce retention, task shifting and medical deserts3; actions on skills development under the BeWell project4, projects on training programmes and digital skills5 and an action on shortages of nurses6. The Cohesion Policy Funds7,8 and the Recovery and Resilience Facility9 may provide additional support.

The Commission supports Member States via the EU Drugs Strategy 2021-202510 and its Action Plan11, which identify the priorities, including on health-related aspects of drug use and drug-related harm. Strengthening access to treatment and care services including evidence-based targeted prevention interventions for people who use drugs is a priority area12.

The EU Drugs Agency promotes evidence-based interventions to raise awareness on the adverse effects of drugs13. The Commission is evaluating the implementation of the Strategy and its Action Plan. The Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-203014 calls on Member States to implement good practices of deinstitutionalisation.

EU labour law15 sets a broad range of minimum requirements to be transposed in national law.
